Adult Stout eelblenny (Anisarchus medius) collected in the Barents Sea during benthic trawl surveys have been recorded attaining a maximum total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], making this one of the larger-bodied zoarcids in the region. Field measurements indicate that individuals reach the onset of gonadal activity at a comparatively modest body size, with the total length at puberty reported at approximately 9.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 9.5 centimeters]. This length threshold is consistent with the general pattern observed among high-latitude eelpouts, where maturation occurs at a size representing roughly one-third of the species' ultimate length, a life-history trait that likely reflects the strong selective pressure to initiate reproduction before the brief Arctic summer window closes. The relationship between length and mass in this species, derived from regional morphometric equations, indicates that a fish of this pubertal length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of about 2.5 grams [Wwp = about 2.5 grams], a relatively modest body mass that underscores the energetic constraints operating on these sub-Arctic benthic fishes.

Reproductive output in Stout eelblenny is tightly coupled to the cold thermal regime of its environment. At the consistently low water temperatures characteristic of its deep Arctic habitat, approximately -0.6 °C [T = -0.6 °C], females exhibit a maximum daily reproductive rate equivalent to roughly 2 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 2 eggs per day], a value that appears modest in absolute terms but is comparatively high for a zoarcid of this body size living under near-freezing conditions. This elevated rate is sustained over the spawning season and is facilitated by the production of relatively small, yolk-rich oocytes. Studies examining batch fecundity in gravid females reveal that individuals produce between 1 and 3 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = between 1 and 3 eggs per spawning event], with multiple clutches laid across the reproductive period at a frequency of approximately 2 spawning events per day [F_R_i = approximately 2 spawning events per day] during the peak of summer when food availability is highest.

The early life stages of Anisarchus medius are characterized by a relatively prolonged period of embryonic development, a consequence of the species' adaptation to sub-zero temperatures. Eggs incubated at a stable thermal regime of -0.6 °C [T = -0.6 °C] require an incubation period of 170 days [ab = 170 days] before eclosion occurs, a duration that is among the longest documented for any Arctic marine teleost and which reflects the profoundly retarded metabolic rates imposed by the cold environment. Upon hatching, the yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of roughly 2 millimeters and consistent with the allometric scaling relationships typical of the family Zoarcidae. This small initial mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding, as the endogenous yolk reserves are limited and must sustain the larva through the critical period of mouth opening and first prey capture.

Growth trajectories documented from otolith increment analysis indicate that adult Stout eelblenny continue to increase in mass throughout their lives, eventually approaching an ultimate wet weight of 74 grams [Wwi = 74 grams] at the asymptotic length of 30 centimeters. This maximum body mass, derived from length-weight regressions specific to Barents Sea populations, represents a substantial increase of several orders of magnitude from the hatchling mass and implies a sustained period of somatic investment. The species' pace of life is notably slow, with estimates of maximum longevity from capture-mark-recapture studies and validated otolith readings suggesting that individuals can reach a lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of -0.6 °C [T = -0.6 °C]. This remarkably extended lifespan, more than double that of many temperate eelpout species of comparable size, is a classic hallmark of life in perennially cold waters, where reduced metabolic demands and delayed senescence allow for prolonged reproductive windows and iterative spawning over many seasons.

Comparative ecological analyses place the Stout eelblenny within a slow life-history continuum among Arctic benthic fishes, a suite of traits that also includes delayed maturation and high adult survival. The species' ultimate total length of 30 centimeters distinguishes it from smaller sympatric zoarcids such as Lycodes reticulatus, while its total length at puberty of 9.5 centimeters represents a relatively high degree of somatic investment prior to first breeding. Field observations conducted near Svalbard indicate that the daily reproductive rate of roughly 2 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 2 eggs per day] is sustained across a spawning period that extends through the summer months, with the associated wet weight at puberty of about 2.5 grams representing the threshold mass at which resources are redirected toward gametogenesis. The interplay between these life-history parameters, set against the backdrop of a 13-year lifespan, suggests that Anisarchus medius employs a bet-hedging strategy in which reproductive effort is spread across many seasons to buffer against the stochastic recruitment success typical of high-latitude marine environments.
